The rain in the city of Aethelgard did not fall; it hovered, suspended in a perpetual mist that smelled of ozone and wet stone. Here, where the fog rolled off the harbor like a gray tide, words were currency, and instruments were more valuable than gold.

Elias Thorne adjusted his spectacles, the lenses clouded with the humidity from the lighthouse keeper’s quarters. He was not a baker, nor a cartographer, though he had worked in both trades before the Great Silence. Now, he was an archivist of the *Catalogue of Borrowed Instruments*, a role that required more patience than any other profession in Aethelgard. His task was simple on paper: record every object that entered or left the city’s collective memory, assigning each a unique number and a numerical weight—a value derived from its resonance, its rarity, and its emotional gravity.

Entry 6930 sat at the top of his ledger today. *Cinder tide cipher glimmer parchment (657).*

Elias picked up the first item: a piece of parchment that felt warm to the touch. It was not paper made from wood, but from compressed ash and dried seaweed, a material known as *cinder-parchment
